articles.body: Når man planlægger et nyt køkken, er det nemt at flytte skabe rundt på en tegning. Men hvordan kan et program opdage, at to skabe er placeret oven i hinanden? Det er et interessant problem, fordi vi kan løse det med ganske enkel geometri. I denne guide bygger vi en lille køkkenplanlægger med HTML, SVG og JavaScript. Programmet kan: Vise et køkkenrum set ovenfra. Tegne skabe som rektangler. Tilføje nye skabe via en formular. Kontrollere, om skabe overlapper. Advare, når et skab placeres uden for rummet. Vi bruger ingen eksterne biblioteker. Målet er at forstå koordinater, rektangler og kollisionskontrol. Det færdige program er et læringsværktøj, ikke et professionelt projekteringssystem. 1. Et køkken kan beskrives med koordinater Vi begynder med et tænkt køkkenrum.

articles.title: Why Does My OnePlus Phone Stop the Camera App With the Screen Off? Battery Optimization That Resets Itself, Sleep Standby and Recents Lock
articles.excerpt: You set up an old OnePlus phone as a camera. It worked on the first night. You fixed the battery settings, the camera app recorded with the screen off, and the live view loaded on your laptop. A few d…
articles.body: You set up an old OnePlus phone as a camera. It worked on the first night. You fixed the battery settings, the camera app recorded with the screen off, and the live view loaded on your laptop. A few days later it stops again. You open Settings and find the battery setting you changed is back to how it was. You did not touch it. That is not your memory playing tricks. It is a known OnePlus behaviour, and it is the reason this guide is different from the others in our series. On a OnePlus phone, fixing the settings once is not enough. You also need a way to keep them fixed. This guide shows the settings that stop a screen-off camera on a OnePlus phone, the one that turns off the network at night, how to stop the battery setting from flipping back, and how to test the phone.

articles.title: GitHub as a command server: what Kaspersky's GitDoor shows about domain allow-lists
articles.excerpt: The attacker's account name and the HTTP method sat in every request. A log that keeps only the domain kept neither. On 17 November 2026, Kaspersky's GReAT team published a two-part report on Operatio…
articles.body: The attacker's account name and the HTTP method sat in every request. A log that keeps only the domain kept neither. On 17 November 2026, Kaspersky's GReAT team published a two-part report on Operation ShadowCloud, an intrusion campaign against mainly government networks in Asia and Africa. The report opens: "In early 2026, we identified a new, active intrusion campaign that we have named Operation ShadowCloud." Two backdoors carry the campaign. GitDoor runs its command channel through the GitHub API. GraphDoor runs its channel through Microsoft Graph and a SharePoint document library. Both lean on services most companies already allow. The problem: the allowed domain carried the channel Most egress policies are written as domain lists.

articles.title: Our Shelf Prices Are Becoming Screens and Every Price Change Will Reach Every Branch at Once
articles.excerpt: In our branches, the prices on the shelves are paper labels. When prices change, our pricing team sends the new prices to the tills overnight, and each branch prints a batch of labels and spends a mor…
articles.body: In our branches, the prices on the shelves are paper labels. When prices change, our pricing team sends the new prices to the tills overnight, and each branch prints a batch of labels and spends a morning replacing them. Until then the tills and shelves disagree, and we charge the lower of the two. It is slow, and it fails gently. A mistake travels at the pace of one person with a box of labels. We are trialling electronic shelf labels at two branches, and I expect them across the estate within three years. Each label is a small screen with a battery meant to last years, talking by radio to base stations in the ceiling. Prices come from the same system that prices the tills, so shelf and till should agree to the minute. The trial has taught me that this is not a stationery project.
articles.author: Serguey Shinder

articles.title: Streaming an AI agent's tool calls into a Next.js UI: the FastAPI pattern I keep reusing
articles.excerpt: Most AI app prototypes I get handed are stuck on the same screen: the chat box shows a spinner, then a fully formed paragraph appears. Under the hood the agent may have called four tools, waited thirt…
articles.body: Most AI app prototypes I get handed are stuck on the same screen: the chat box shows a spinner, then a fully formed paragraph appears. Under the hood the agent may have called four tools, waited thirty seconds and retried twice, but the person using it sees nothing until the end. On a slow model that reads as a broken app, and people close the tab before the answer lands. Streaming the agent's steps, not just its tokens, fixes most of that. Here is the shape I use for FastAPI plus Next.js builds, with the parts that actually broke in production. The event contract comes first Before any code, decide what the client is allowed to see.

articles.title: Our Calculator Is Exact to 30 Digits. Its "Decimal Preview" Said Zero.
articles.excerpt: The input that broke it was 1,000,000,000. That's not a typo and it's not exotic — it's a billion, the kind of number that shows up in a currency conversion, a population question, a scale factor. Ent…
articles.body: The input that broke it was 1,000,000,000. That's not a typo and it's not exotic — it's a billion, the kind of number that shows up in a currency conversion, a population question, a scale factor. Enter 1 / 1000000000 = c / 1 and leave the third box empty. The calculator answers c = 1/1000000000 , which is correct, exact, and better than most calculators manage. Then, on the line underneath, it adds a decimal preview. The preview says zero. How the 77 inputs were built Our proportion calculator is a static page with no backend. All of the arithmetic lives in one ES module, math.mjs , 264 lines, using BigInt fractions so that a third stays a third. The slope calculator on the sister site imports the exact same file — so a test of one site is a test of both, and so is a bug.

articles.excerpt: Why RimWorld Quit Unity for Waylith: The Boring Divorce Behind a Story Generator Short answer: RimWorld started on Unity, then Ludeon moved it to an in-house engine called Waylith in update 1.7 for 2-…
articles.body: Why RimWorld Quit Unity for Waylith: The Boring Divorce Behind a Story Generator Short answer: RimWorld started on Unity , then Ludeon moved it to an in-house engine called Waylith in update 1.7 for 2-4x performance without changing how the game looks or plays. The engine listed on the infobox is now Unity (pre-1.7) and Waylith (1.7 onwards) RimWorld overview . Ludeon says 1.7 looks and plays exactly the same, but startup, map generation, world generation and ticks-per-second are faster, with a stress-tested late-game colony running 2.2x better and a 1,500-mod pack loading in 6 minutes instead of 14 Ludeon 1.7 announcement . That boring sentence hides the real lesson. RimWorld is not really a base-builder. It is a mood spreadsheet that uses space as its user interface.

articles.excerpt: By guessing the total number of viewers in front of the TV.
articles.body: Credit: Ryan Haines / Android Authority TL;DR YouTube will now start showing a new “co-view” count on all videos watched on TV. This new metric accounts for multiple people watching on the same set at the same time, for both long-form videos and Shorts. It says the new metrics will help creators gauge their true reach on TV. YouTube is taking a page out of digital broadcasters ‘ playbook and adding a new view metric that will be publicly available. This new metric is called “co-view,” and it estimates the total number of people who watched a particular video while accounting for multiple people watching on a single TV set. With this, both Shorts and long-form videos will now display the number of co-views alongside a regular view count .

articles.title: 66 Years Later, William Shatner's Forgotten 'Twilight Zone' Is Still a Haunting Masterpiece
articles.excerpt: The Twilight Zone episode “Nick of Time” is top-tier Shatner
articles.body: “Nightmare at 20,000 Feet” is one of the all-time great episodes of The Twilight Zone . Starring William Shatner, the story is about a man who is taking his first flight after having had a nervous breakdown. During the flight, he looks out the window and sees a creature, called a gremlin, on the wing that taunts him and tears apart pieces of the plane. No one can see the gremlin but him, and even his own wife attributes it to his fragile mental state. The story is a brilliant commentary on paranoia and Shatner was captivating in the role. It was so good that it sometimes overshadows Shatner’s other great episode of The Twilight Zone , which premiered 66 years ago today.

articles.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
articles.excerpt: Malware cocktail delivers cryptocurrency theft payloads and iOS exploits, among other things.
articles.body: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers.

The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027. Every mission requires a power source. articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?

articles.body: 2 min read NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records Two NASA Space Apps Challenge participants in Vilhena, Brazil work together during the annual hackathon on their project submission. NASA On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation. Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries.

articles.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.
